newsitem.title: GERMANY: Duisenberg - no tight rate policy at EMU start.
newsitem.headline: Duisenberg - no tight rate policy at EMU start.

text.p: Dutch central bank president Wim Duisenberg, president elect of the European Monetary Institute (EMI), said on Thursday the future European Central Bank (ECB) should not need a tight rate policy at the start.
In an interview with Germany's Manager Magazine, released in advance of publication, Duisenberg said the current trend toward low interest rates in Europe was likely to continue.

Asked if there was a risk that the ECB would follow a very tight rate policy to prove its independence after the euro launch, Duisenberg said: "I don't think this will be necessary. We are currently observing a totally different trend. Interest rates are moving toward low German or Dutch levels everywhere."
"This process will continue, because markets can expect that there will be continuity on currency policy after 1999," he added.
Duisenberg added that European central bankers were keen to see inflation at a rate of between zero and two percent.
Asked about the fact Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan appeared to be happy with an inflation rate of 2.5 to three percent, Duisenberg said: "Less is better."

Duisenberg is due to take over from Alexandre Lamfalussy as the EMI president on July 1 and is widely viewed as the top candidate to head up the ECB, which will guide monetary policy in the euro zone once the single currency is launched, as planned, on January 1 1999.
Duisenberg also said the ECB was not in any danger of being influenced by politicians once it starts operations.

"The central bank will be, according to the Maastricht Treaty, significantly more independent than the Bundesbank or the Dutch central bank, more independent than any central bank that I know in the world," he said.
He conceded that individual governments might try to exert influence on the central bank.
"But that won't do any good. They would have to exert succcesful pressure on a central bank council which contains a possible 15 people, each of whom is in turn obliged to be independent."
Europeans need have no fear that European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) will carry hidden risks, he said.
"I am convinced that Europeans need have no fear of the euro. Because it has been ensured that the risks are very limited," he said.
